producers.note: CBPP's blog of 16 September 2026, 'Official Poverty Measure and Anchored Supplemental Poverty Measure Show Poverty Rate Declined in 2025', restates Census's FCSUti-anchored SPM ('By Census' anchored SPM, the poverty rate fell to 12.6 percent in 2025, from 13.0 percent in 2024', citing SEHSD-WP2026-22) and says the lagged spending factor added 'a sizeable 0.5 percentage points to the poverty rate'. The figures are Census's FCSUti-anchored rates, staged from the Census paper under open_search. The blog returns HTTP 403 (a Cloudflare challenge) to direct fetches and has no Wayback capture, so it was read only through a reader proxy (r.jina.ai) and is not staged (harvest rule 8). The 10 September preview (9-10-26pov.pdf, read) has no estimate: it expected the SPM to rise because thresholds rose 4.4 to 6.3 percent. Parrott's statement of 15 September (9-15-26pov-stmt.pdf, read) has no anchored figure. CBPP's live blog 'Analyzing the Census Bureau's 2025 Poverty, Income, and Health Insurance Data' (16 September; read through the same proxy) excerpts the anchored post and links to it, with no further figure on these quantities.

Its charts label only 1967 and 2025; Figure 1 Panel B labels 2025 at 13.1 percent, the published rate. Panel B also plots an unlabelled 2024 point: a 2024 rate at 2025 real thresholds, which the post does not estimate, and a change taken from it would be derived from two numbers (harvest rule 1). The databook prints no 2025 rate at 2024 thresholds, no 2024-to-2025 change and no threshold effect, so there is no figure on the post's quantities. producers.note: Census SEHSD-WP2026-22 (DiTommaso, released with P60-290 on 15 September 2026) is the one comparable: Table A.4 anchors the 2024 thresholds with CPI-U, the post's own world (staged and compared), and Tables A.2 and A.3 with the FCSUti price index (staged, annotated concept_mismatch). Only the rows the post estimates are staged (all people, under 18, 18 to 64, 65 and over, and the three tenure groups' 2025 rates); the sex, race, education and work rows, the tenure changes and the 2024 and 2025 production columns (Census's published rates, survey levels) are not. P60-290 states only that faster growth in the threshold's components raises SPM thresholds more than CPI-U would; SEHSD-WP2026-09 (Creamer, May 2026) runs to 2024; the 9 September Census blog predates the data; CRS IN12737 (16 September 2026) describes the difference in threshold updating in words, with no figure; the Center for American Progress (15 September 2026) restates BLS's 4.4 to 6.3 percent threshold growth with no poverty effect; Winship's 'How Not to Redefine Poverty' is from November 2025. Cato's 16 September blog (Boccia and Turman; direct fetch blocked by an Incapsula challenge, read via the Wayback Machine) argues that SPM thresholds rise in real terms and gives the 2025 official and SPM rates, with no figure on the post's quantities. A New Mexico legislative handout on the poverty release returned 404 and is out of scope for a federal analysis.
